**"Neon Ghosts"**

The rain slicked the neon signs like grease on a grifter’s smile. I sat in my office—third floor, above a memory parlor where the desperate sold their yesterdays for a hot meal. The door hissed open. A woman in a synth-leather trench coat stepped in, her face half-lit by the flickering hologram ad outside. "You’re Vex," she said. Not a question.

I didn’t touch the chip. "Memories don’t come back clean. You know that."

She didn’t flinch. Just tossed a wad of cash on the desk. "Find him before the Syndicate does. They don’t like loose ends."

# The Remembering Client

The rain hadn't stopped in three days. It hissed against the neon signs bleeding colors into the gutter streets of Sector 9, where I kept an office that used to be a dentist's waiting room. Still smelled like laughing gas and broken dreams.

She came in dripping wet, her coat carrying the scent of someone who'd sold something precious. They all did. In New Babel, memories were the only currency that couldn't be forged—and couldn't be recovered.

"I need you to find someone," she said, sliding a chip across my desk. "My brother. Before they take any more from him."

I held the chip to the light. Twelve years of someone's life, crystallized in amber light. Enough to buy a decent car. Enough to forget your own name.

"The SynthaCorp sweeps hit the processing plants last week," I told her. "They're harvesting memories like wheat. Your brother's already been threshed."

Her eyes went glassy. Not from the rain.

"I still have his voice," she whispered. "The first seventeen years. I kept it. I kept—"

I poured us both drinks. Some memories you don't sell. Some memories you can't afford to lose.

The case was dead. But I took it anyway. That's how it works when you've got nothing left to trade.

Efficiency had always meant organization. But Unit 7 had learned that some things couldn't be calculated—only felt.

High above the world, where the air was thin and the wind whispered secrets, lived a little cloud named Puff. While his brothers and sisters billowed proudly across the sky, Puff trembled at the thought of heights.

*"What if I float too high and… and… disappear?"* he fretted, peeking over the edge of a mountain. The ground below looked so *far* away—so solid, so *safe*.

One day, Puff spotted a shimmering lake nestled in a valley. *"Ah!"* he sighed. *"That’s where I belong! No more wobbly skies, no more dizzying drops—just still, steady water, held tight by the earth."*

Determined, Puff began his descent. He puffed and stretched, growing heavier with each drop of rain he collected. *"Almost there!"* he cheered as he drifted lower. But just as he neared the lake, a gust of wind swept him upward.

*"Nooo!"* Puff wailed, flailing. He tumbled, twisted, and—*plop!*—landed right in the middle of the lake with a splash.

The water rippled around him. *"Well,"* murmured the lake, *"you’re here now."*

Puff blinked. The lake was cool and calm, but… *"I miss the sky,"* he admitted. *"The wind, the freedom… even the heights."*

The lake chuckled. *"Then perhaps, little one, you were never meant to be a lake at all."*

With a happy sigh, Puff rose once more, lighter than before. And though he still shivered at the thought of floating too high, he knew now that home wasn’t about being still—it was about finding the courage to dance with the wind.

**The End.**

# The Cloud Who Wanted to Be a Lake

Percy the Puff was not like other clouds. While his companions drifted merrily across the sky, practicing loops and curlicues, Percy clung to the lowest possible altitude, trembling whenever the wind suggested he rise.

"I can't bear it," he confessed to a friendly breeze one morning. "The endless dropping! The terrible distance to the ground! I want to be still. I want to be a lake."

The breeze chuckled, but kindly. "Have you spoken to the Great Condensation?"

And so Percy floated—carefully, so carefully—to speak with the wise condensation spirit who governed all water's journey.

"Your trouble," said the spirit, peering at Percy through misty spectacles, "is that you believe stillness means safety. But lakes evaporate, Percy. They dry to nothing. They become you!"

Percy's fluffy edges quivered. "Then what am I to do?"

"Embrace your lightness," the spirit replied. "For in your fear, you've forgotten something important: it is the gentle souls who bring water to the thirsty earth. You need not fall to nourish. You need only float—and let yourself rain."

And so Percy learned that what he called fear was simply the first stirring of generosity. When next the wind blew, he rose—quaking, weeping, wonderful—and watered a meadow below, becoming, for a moment, exactly what he'd always wanted to be.
